newsitem.title: KENYA: Opposition disrupts Kenya budget speech.
newsitem.headline: Opposition disrupts Kenya budget speech.

text.p: Kenyan opposition members of parliament disrupted Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi's budget speech on Thursday with noisy demands for constitutional reforms.
With President Daniel arap Moi inside the chamber, Mudavadi tried to make himself heard above the din when state television stopped its live coverage without explanation.
Waving banners saying "No Reforms, No Budget", the opposition parliamentarians stamped their feet and shouted, drowning out Mudavadi's speech.
The government imposed tight security in central Nairobi to foil opposition plans for a protest rally outside parliament.
Hundreds of police, backed by the feared anti-riot General Service Unit (GSU), deployed at strategic points in and around the capital.
Armed with wooden staves, shields and teargas canisters, they sealed off the parliament building.
With political tension rising in the East African country, the protest was eventually staged inside the British-style parliament instead of on the streets.
Opposition members snubbed Moi at the start of the session, declining to stand when he entered the chamber.
The speaker, Francis Ole Kaparo, repeatedly cried "Order, Order" and appealed to the opposition to behave.
Kaparo earlier refused opposition member James Orengo's request for a debate on proposed constitutional reforms before elections at an unspecified date this year.
The normally bustling city centre was semi-deserted.
Shops as well as some schools and offices were closed with people fearing a violent confrontation between the security forces and activists demanding political reforms.
Shopkeepers, many of whom are of Indian and Pakistani descent, feared a repeat of two days of looting after an opposition rally was forcibly dispersed by police on May 31.
"We are closing early because we are scared," said shop owner Megufa Delve.
"We are going to close today because of total insecurity. We have moved all goods from display windows already," said Japrakash Mishra of retail chain Nakumatt.

Police cleared civilians for a radius of several hundred metres (yards) when Moi arrived at parliament for Mudavadi's 1997/98 budget speech. His first attempt to read it began about one hour behind schedule.
City centre banks remained open and the shilling was stable. Business on the Nairobi Stock Exchange was sluggish with some brokers closing 15 minutes early.
Some staff at the downtown U.S. embassy stayed away from work, heeding advice not to come if they feared trouble.
Moi has agreed to relax a tough law restricting public assemblies but ruled out any more constitutional reforms until after general elections to be held this year.
Moi, 73 this year, looks certain to extend his 19-year rule for another five years, both because of the existing electoral rules and the deep personal and ethnic splits within the opposition.
A Western diplomat said the government was set to announce a concession by extending the registration of voters nationwide by two weeks from the original deadline of June 22.
The National Electoral Commission said on Wednesday it had so far registered only 5.1 million voters, half the estimated electorate in the country of nearly 30 million.
Despite the ban on the opposition rally, hundreds of supporters of Moi's ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) were allowed to gather in central Nairobi, chanting praise for the government.
Some told reporters they had been paid by KANU to disrupt the NCA march to parliament.
"We do not need a permit to march because we are on the side of KANU. We are working with the police and we are ready to disrupt the opposition march," KANU official Joseph Nyakunde said.
